items.title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
items.content: arXiv:2611.17762v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.

This addresses the gap between unconstrained creative T2I generation and the implicit, product-specific constraints of real industrial design.
items.reasoning: A targeted applied contribution combining existing techniques (T2I, self-enhancement loops) for a niche industrial use case; useful but not methodologically novel.

items.title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
items.content: arXiv:2611.17802v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.

This supports personalized service in domestic and office robotics.

items.title: Classifier-Guided Latent Diffusion for Small-Molecule Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.17650v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a promising class of generative models for molecular design because of their ability to learn complex chemical distributions and support conditional or guided generation. In this work, we investigate a latent diffusion pipeline for property-guided small-molecule generation. The proposed framework represents canonicalized SMILES strings using a frozen ChemBERTa encoder, trains a Transformer-based decoder to reconstruct SELFIES strings from molecular latent embeddings, and learns an unconditional denoising diffusion model in the ChemBERTa latent space. To enable property-directed generation, a differentiable latent property predictor is used to guide the diffusion sampling process. Generated SELFIES strings are converted to SMILES, validated using RDKit, and evaluated using molecular validity, uniqueness, novelty, and predicted property scores. We study guidance toward two drug-relevant binary endpoints: blood--brain barrier permeability and inhibition of human $\beta$-secretase 1. The results suggest that latent diffusion over pretrained molecular embeddings can generate chemically valid and novel molecules while enabling controllable steering toward desired molecular properties.

items.summary: The authors build a latent diffusion pipeline for property-guided small-molecule generation using a frozen ChemBERTa encoder, a Transformer decoder mapping latents to SELFIES, and a differentiable property predictor guiding sampling. This applies established diffusion guidance ideas to molecular design. Results appear to validate chemically valid, property-directed generation.
items.reasoning: Competent but largely combinational work assembling known components (ChemBERTa latents, diffusion, classifier guidance) for drug discovery; likely modest quantitative gains and limited novelty for a general AI audience.

items.title: Small Is Not Dead: Distance-Aware Cluster Revival for e-means
items.content: arXiv:2611.18238v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) is a recent mini-batch k-means algorithm, now part of the FAISS library, that reaches the error of Lloyd's algorithm about an order of magnitude faster on large embedding datasets. Every five mini-batches, it removes every cluster whose running point count falls below a tenth of the average and reuses its centre to split a large cluster. In the authors' ablation, removing this mechanism, called dead-cluster revival, raises the error more than removing any other component added to the moving-average update. The rule, however, considers only cluster size: it cannot distinguish a cluster that is small because it is redundant from one that covers a rare, isolated group of points, and on data with such groups it repeatedly removes centres whose removal is costly. We add a second condition, based on the distance between centres: a small cluster is removed only if its centre is close to another centre, relative to a running estimate of the mean squared error. When a centre equals the mean of its points, this squared distance is an upper bound on the average increase in squared error, per point of the cluster, caused by removing the centre. The condition costs one nearest-centre search for the small clusters every five mini-batches and adds no measurable running time. On the e-means paper's embedding benchmarks, it never prevents a removal, so the results are identical to those of FAISS. On datasets with small isolated groups not used during development, it reduces the test error after two epochs by roughly 10% to 80% relative to count-based revival, and it preserves the advantage of k-means++ initialization; on the other evaluation datasets, it stays within about 1% of the better of revival enabled and disabled. We also report two failure modes that the analysis predicts. This is a CPU proof of concept; GPU implementations are left to future work.
items.author: Eyal Weiss
items.summary: The paper improves the e-means mini-batch k-means algorithm's dead-cluster revival mechanism by making it distance-aware, so small clusters covering rare isolated groups are not repeatedly eliminated as redundant. This addresses the single most impactful failure mode identified in the original algorithm's ablations.
items.reasoning: A focused, well-targeted algorithmic fix to a recently deployed clustering method in FAISS; useful for practitioners but incremental in scope and novelty.

items.title: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy
items.content: arXiv:2611.18507v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.

items.summary: This theoretical work studies classification heads built on conic functions whose bounded class regions are used to reject unseen classes, asking whether softmax cross-entropy training keeps features inside those regions. The author derives quadric boundaries for class regions, defines an asymptotic margin computable via second-order cone programs, and characterizes when class loss has infimum zero.
items.reasoning: Careful mathematical analysis of an underexplored architecture family (conic heads for open-set rejection), with connections to optimization via SOCP formulations. The niche topic and single-author scope limit broad impact, but the theory appears rigorous and novel.

items.title: Domain Adaptation Based Pipeline for Character Classification and Handwritten Text Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.17952v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Character classification and handwritten text recognition, particularly in specialized tasks, often suffer from limited labeled data, while a large amount of unlabeled data remains unused. To address this challenge, we propose a novel unsupervised domain adaptation-based pipeline to reduce the distribution gap between source and target domains. Our pipeline follows three main steps. In the first step, we pretrained an expert model on source data, to learn a strong general representation. In the second step, we perform unsupervised domain adaptation to leverage unlabeled target data, adapting the model to the specific characteristics of the target domain. In the third step, we trained the expert model on source data in the target style. By aligning the feature distributions between the source and target, our method enables the model to generalize effectively across diverse datasets. The unsupervised training increases the computation time only during training not in inference. We evaluate the pipeline on both character-level and historical handwritten line recognition tasks, demonstrating its flexibility. We establish a new state-of-the-art on the Safran-MNIST-DLS dataset defined in Track 2 of the DAGECC competition with 76.17% Macro F1-score and achieve competitive results on each of the specific datasets of READ 2018 without using the labels of the target data. Code is available at https://github.com/simon-corbi/DRANet-for-classification-and-htr
items.author: Florent Imbert, Simon Corbill\'e, Hui Han, Elisa H. Barney Smith
items.summary: The authors propose a three-step unsupervised domain adaptation pipeline for handwritten text recognition: pretraining an expert model on source data, adapting to unlabeled target data, then training on restyled source data. This targets specialized historical or domain-specific handwriting tasks where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data abounds.
items.reasoning: A competent application-level contribution combining established domain adaptation techniques for handwriting recognition. Useful for digital humanities and document analysis communities, but the pipeline is incremental rather than methodologically novel.

items.title: CamSpokenNLI: A Pilot Resource for Cross-Variety Transfer Evaluation in Cameroon Pidgin English and Camfranglais
items.content: arXiv:2611.17573v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Cameroon Pidgin English (a West African Pidgin English variety) and Camfranglais are widely used in Cameroon, yet to our knowledge, neither has a dedicated spoken Natural Language Inference (NLI) resource. We introduce CamSpokenNLI, a pilot dataset of 114 scenario-matched spoken NLI items in each variety (228 in total), recorded by one native speaker from Buea. Each item pairs premise audio and text with a hypothesis, an NLI label, and English glosses. The author assigned labels, so the dataset is an exploratory resource rather than a mature benchmark. The NLI experiments use the reference text; the audio is evaluated separately. XLM-RoBERTa baselines with five-fold item-level cross-validation reach 44.7% on Pidgin and 46.2% on Camfranglais (chance 33.3%). Still, neither is statistically distinguishable from hypothesis-only input, so hypothesis wording may account for much of the accuracy. Under disjoint-item cross-variety transfer, where a test item's counterpart is never seen in training, accuracy is 40.1% (Pidgin to Camfranglais) and 45.6% (Camfranglais to Pidgin). A counterpart-leak audit raises this to 60-64%, illustrating how counterpart leakage can overstate transfer. Zero-shot Whisper transcription of the recordings performs poorly: the best word error rates are 66.6% for Pidgin and 45.5% for Camfranglais, and with automatic language identification, Whisper Large-v3 labels 93 of 114 Pidgin recordings as Yoruba or Swahili. Together, the results suggest that such resources need disjoint-item evaluation and hypothesis-only controls, and that speech recognition must be adapted to these varieties before spoken NLI can be tested end to end.

items.summary: CamSpokenNLI is a pilot spoken natural language inference dataset for Cameroon Pidgin English and Camfranglais, with 114 scenario-matched items per variety including premise audio and text, hypotheses, labels, and English glosses. XLM-RoBERTa baselines reach only around 45-46 percent accuracy, underscoring how poorly current models handle these varieties. As a single-annotator pilot it is explicitly exploratory rather than a mature benchmark.
items.reasoning: Valuable for linguistic diversity and low-resource NLP, filling a genuine resource gap for understudied African language varieties. However, the tiny size (228 items), single native-speaker annotator, and pilot status limit reliability and immediate impact.

Together, the results suggest that such resources need disjoint-item evaluation and hypothesis-only controls, and that speech recognition must be adapted to these varieties before spoken NLI can be tested end to end.

items.title: Toward Universal Translatability: On the Statistical Ontology of Generative AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.17963v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper argues that the problem of translation functions both as a point of origin and as a normative horizon for contemporary generative AI. In current discourse around ''world models,'' their attainment is framed as the achievement of internal consistency, cross-modal alignment, and physical grounding. Taken together, these demands converge on an ideal of the model as a universal translation machine capable of establishing lossless correspondences across linguistic, visual, and physical representation spaces. I show that this ideal presupposes a metaphysical commitment that I call a statistical ontology: the belief that reality has an underlying, computable statistical structure that can be recovered through sufficient data and modeling, rather than being shaped and accessed through situated human interpretation and labor. Tracing this commitment back to Warren Weaver's 1949 Memorandum on machine translation, I outline how translation was historically recast as code deciphering and, later, as the alignment of probability distributions across structured outputs. Finally, I contrast this paradigm with approaches in Translation Studies that foreground opacity, power asymmetries, and the translator's positionality. I argue that generative AI's statistical ontology is pre-Kantian, pre-critical and obscures the infrastructures and human labor that make machine translatability---as alignment---possible in the first place.

items.title: EViDS: An Environment--Vehicle Dynamics Integrated Simulation Platform for Intelligent Chassis Development
items.content: arXiv:2611.17660v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The development of intelligent chassis increasingly requires the integration of environmental and perception information with high-fidelity vehicle dynamics to support environment-aware intelligent chassis control. However, existing autonomous-driving simulators and professional vehicle-dynamics tools are generally developed for different purposes, making it difficult to integrate environmental information, vehicle dynamics, and chassis algorithms. This paper proposes EViDS, an Environment-Vehicle Dynamics Integrated Simulation Platform for Intelligent Chassis Development. EViDS integrates CARLA-based environment and sensor simulation with CarSim-based high-fidelity vehicle dynamics. Reference-pose-based state alignment and multi-rate interaction maintain spatial and temporal consistency, while ray-casting-based tire-road interaction transfers environmental information to the vehicle-dynamics model. Scenario configuration, synchronized data acquisition, and algorithm interfaces further support intelligent chassis development. The platform is evaluated through environment-dynamics interaction tests with vehicle-dynamics consistency comparisons, together with intelligent chassis applications. Results show that EViDS preserves vehicle-dynamics characteristics, reliably transfers environmental information, and supports online closed-loop intelligent chassis control, providing a unified simulation basis for environment-aware intelligent chassis development and validation.

items.title: Node Localization by Multidimensional Scaling with Iterative Majorization
items.content: arXiv:2611.18466v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Node localization aims to estimate the positions of nodes based on collected data from other nodes. Depending on the data characteristics, different procedures are utilized to estimate the locations. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive multidimensional scaling algorithm based on iterative majorization that comprises many of the different data characteristics to estimate node locations. The implicitly normalized loss function provides absolute distances and, given anchors, absolute node locations. The algorithm uses a new convergent coordinate descent procedure for the minimization of the majorization function, allowing for a natural treatment of anchors. Optimal transformations of the data seamlessly allows other data than Euclidean distances. Data from multiple sources, resulting in either asymmetric or three-way data, fit the same extensive framework.

items.summary: The paper introduces a comprehensive multidimensional scaling algorithm based on iterative majorization for node localization that handles many data characteristics within one framework. items.reasoning: A solid classical-statistics algorithmic contribution relevant to sensor network localization, but it is an incremental methodological refinement outside mainstream AI research interest.

items.title: Where ASI Could Stumble
items.content:
Before our eyes, forecasts are contracting and RSI is becoming nearer with each day. That's why I decided to publish a wide list of the obstacles for AI progress. I've been collecting these ideas for a long time, trying to make the list as comprehensive as it can be.

Some of these obstacles may turn out to be almost irrelevant. Others might slow things down by months or even longer. Or they might not. It's difficult to estimate their impact, so for now my goal was just to briefly list them.

List will include more then just obvious things like market correction, hardware shortages, or diminishing returns. Those are here too, of course. But also there are a few things that don't get a lot of attention.

I will start with the ones I consider as less interesting (part I) and move on to the more unusual variants (parts II & III).

# I. Physical and Economic Bottlenecks

## 1. Energy limits

Developers announce campuses in gigawatts, file for interconnection and publish target dates that rarely survive permitting, financing and power supply.

- Energy Aspects

## 2. Hardware limits

IDC expects industry wafer capacity to grow by about 80% in 2027, while demand grows close to 2x.

- IDC

## 3. Market correction

Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction.

- IMF

## 4. Lack of training data

Actually, I don't personally consider this as a bottleneck. AI could learn from synthetic data or simulations without running into model collapse. We might also discover ways to train models more efficiently on the data we already have. Systems with continuous learning may emerge. After all, humans still generate thousands of petabytes of new data every day.

### Additional:

There's also a tacit knowledge: knowledge that hasn't been formalized and is therefore difficult to transfer. But there's an obvious objection: AI can generalize beyond its training data. The real question is how well it can do that....

items.summary: A comprehensive taxonomic list of obstacles that could slow AI progress toward superintelligence, spanning energy limits, hardware/wafer capacity shortfalls, market corrections, and diminishing returns, plus less-discussed bottlenecks the author flags as unusual. Explicitly aims for breadth over impact estimation.
items.reasoning: A useful reference compilation of progress bottlenecks with some cited sources (IDC, energy interconnection data), relevant to forecasting debates about timelines. However, it is an itemized list without quantitative analysis of which constraints bind, and acknowledges it cannot estimate impact.

items.title: On the Brutality of Amdahl's Law
items.content:
Following my 3-week visit to Berkeley as described here and featured by ACX here, I told various people I would write in detail why I didn’t stick around to work in AI safety. In this post, I will dance around one object-level disagreement with AI safety and rationalists: why I no longer believe in explosive world transformation due to ASI. There will eventually be follow-up pieces on more object-level arguments and meta-level arguments against AI safety, but I prefer for this post to be mostly self-contained and not explicitly about AI safety.

When I worked in theoretical physics research, I was constantly reminded that if I were just that much smarter and had read that many more papers, I would be able to make the right connection to solve the problem. You are always the bottleneck; it’s always a skill issue. So if you’ve spent the bulk of your conscious life honing your ability to manipulate the pure abstraction of math and computer code, it is staggering to watch the problems you wrestled with for months or years get blown away in hours. You are left wondering how quickly all of the other problems in the world will be resolved - all of disease perhaps? Why not all of biology? Why not all the secrets of the universe?

In December 2025 when Claude Code + Opus 4.5 first made agents feel extremely useful, I was concerned about the job market being obliterated, so I took out “insurance” on rapid-onset white-collar unemployment. Thankfully, those predictions about increasingly capable agents causing rapid economic and labor transformation have been very wrong.

And so the question is, why? Why does the world largely look the same outside of highly verifiable domains like software engineering and math, and even in software engineering, why are there still millions employed? Why are models which can beat humans on nearly all benchmarks and are provided at unbelievably low prices not causing large economic shockwaves?...

The author describes the experience of watching AI solve problems that resisted years of human effort and uses that to question bottleneck-centric models of transformative AI impact.

It is still an argumentative essay without empirical work, but it contributes a genuinely contestable object-level position to a key debate.

items.title: What Balanced Accuracy Cannot Identify in Neural-Signal Decoding under Test-Time Adaptation
items.content: arXiv:2611.17925v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Adaptation for neural-signal classification is usually transductive: each batch is scored after updating on it, and the gain depends on the adapted model [4]. This paper asks what an aggregate change fails to characterise inside the cohort. Full test-time adaptation (full_ttt) was evaluated in 11 dataset-encoder cells (four each on Siena/EEG and PTB-XL/ECG, three on Sleep-EDF/EEG), with splits and source-model evaluation fixed; the subject was the unit, exact sign tests were Holm-corrected and conditional on the shared stream, and bootstrap intervals accompanied a dependence audit. Two results of different kinds follow. In the binary case balanced accuracy gives a one-class decoder the same value as one reporting both classes at 50%, so the aggregate cannot identify a class that stopped being reported; a class covering a tenth of a subject's samples went unpredicted in 26-47 of 112 subject-cells, against 7-9 for the controls, which is a descriptive count. With cohort, split and update rule fixed, the within-subject class contrast follows the encoder, tested directly rather than inferred from tests against zero: two of six Siena encoder pairs survive the dependence readings at their nominal reference and one at a fold-level reference, while two of ten Sleep-EDF stage pairs pass the run-clustered gate at its nominal reference; aggregate and contrast named different encoders in 10 of 11. The protocol bounds both results, since a stream-interleaving effect reverses sign with state sharing (+3.5 to -2.4 pp). An aggregate score can hide individual harm, as [1] showed, but it cannot distinguish a uniform loss from a deleted class; class-level change should therefore be reported alongside the aggregate and subject-level change alongside it, with both results conditional on the cell, the rule and the stream construction.

items.summary: This paper shows that balanced accuracy can mask degenerate behavior in test-time adaptation for neural-signal decoding — for example, a one-class decoder can match the balanced accuracy of a genuine decoder at 50% — and characterizes within-cohort effects across 11 dataset-encoder cells on EEG and ECG benchmarks with rigorous corrected sign tests and bootstrap intervals. It provides a methodological caution for TTA evaluation in biosignal classification.
items.reasoning: A rigorous, careful evaluation-methodology critique with good statistical hygiene, but narrowly scoped to neural-signal decoding and primarily a negative result about a metric.

items.title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.17463v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.

items.title: Representational Geometry as a Diagnostic for Adversarial Robustness
items.content: arXiv:2611.17684v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Adversarial training is a common technique for making neural networks more robust to small, intentionally crafted input perturbations, and robustness is commonly measured through accuracy under attack. By exploring inter-network representations across different adversarial training objectives, we can analyze whether multiple networks organize their latent representations similarly. We study Multilayer Perceptrons trained on MNIST under three adversarial training regimes and compare the resulting population training dynamics and geometry to those of a vanilla network. We use M-PHATE to embed data samples across training epochs and examine how the geometry of the data changes during training under adversarial objectives. On penultimate-layer representations we measure displacement between clean and perturbed points, distributional distance through maximum mean discrepancy, and nearest-neighbor recovery. Our visualizations and quantitative analyses show that adversarial training leads to structural changes in how networks organize internal data representations, and robust accuracy and representational stability can rank the same defenses in opposite ways. These findings support a discussion of re-evaluating how practitioners approach the auditing of model robustness by treating latent representations and their training trajectories as diagnostic artifacts across sets of networks.

It offers representational geometry as a diagnostic complement to accuracy-under-attack metrics.

items.title: Deep Neural Networks Training Efficiency: Does Grokking Modify its Dynamics?
items.content: arXiv:2611.18396v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study whether grokking, the delayed emergence of out-of-distribution generalization after apparent overfitting, alters training efficiency in deep neural networks, where efficiency is measured as accuracy per unit energy. Using two canonical settings, modular arithmetic and MNIST, we analyze two neural network models under 16-, 32-, and 64-bit precision and use Orthograd to test whether grokking produces noticeable deviations from the typically decreasing dynamics of training efficiency. We consider both short training runs of up to 500 epochs and long training runs of up to 20,000 epochs, and in both cases identify grokking as a sharp improvement in test accuracy after a sustained train-test gap. In the short-horizon experiments, applying Orthograd at progressively stronger levels during early training does not induce grokking, and efficiency remains smoothly decreasing. In the long-horizon experiments, Orthograd induces grokking, but the efficiency curves remain approximately monotonic and show no appreciable local increase at the grokking transition. These results suggest that, in our setting, grokking does not materially alter overall training-efficiency dynamics.

The short-horizon experiments suggest grokking interacts measurably with energy-efficiency dynamics during training.

items.title: Homogeneous pursuit in $\beta$ model
items.content: arXiv:2611.17609v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Data in forms of networks has been encountered in various prevalent fields at the arrival of big data era. To unveil and recover the true model with core units with numerous links, the $\beta$-model under sparsity constraint is proposed to meet the expectation of statisticians and engineers. Not only does this network model inherit spectacular property from the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi model, but also exhibits degree heterogeneity through tuning sparsity parameter $s$. In this paper, we propose Homogeneous Pursuit (HP), an $\ell_0$-constrained maximum likelihood estimation method implemented through a primal-dual algorithm. To ease the harshness of computation, we find the surrogate function of the corresponding objective function to derive Majorization Minimization algorithm through the primal-dual process. Moreover, after meticulous evaluation, the algorithm brought about captures the property of fine convergence rate in a contraction mapping way. Under some mild conditions, the proposed generalized information criterion (GIC$^*$) for selecting the sparsity level is consistent to find the truth. Combining HP with GIC$^*$ gives the adaptive procedure HP-GIC$^*$; HP-BIC denotes the same estimation method with sparsity selected by BIC. Finally, simulation studies show that GIC$^*$ improves support recovery relative to BIC in the reported comparisons, while HP achieves lower computational cost while maintaining estimation accuracy comparable to the sparse benchmark methods. A microfinance application illustrates the use of HP-GIC$^*$ for studying the association between network prominence and participation, with improved fit in the reported village-level regressions.

items.title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
items.content: arXiv:2611.17781v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.
items.author: Zhuangsheng Li, Yunhan Zhang, Dailin Li, Qingxian Yu, Yu Wu, Youqi Song, Bangyuan He
items.summary: This paper proposes Transition Representation Consistency (TReC), a metric comparing how alternative Go moves change a board-state embedding in a frozen KataGo network, complementing coordinate-distance measures of prediction error. Experiments on 680 mid-to-late-game positions show TReC captures representational differences that raw distance misses. It contributes a representation-level analysis tool for game-playing model behavior.
items.reasoning: A competent but narrow contribution to interpretability of game-playing networks; limited generalizability beyond Go and evaluation is on a single model (KataGo).

items.title: The Transformer Paradigm: Dynamic Processing and a New Principle of Inference
items.content: arXiv:2611.17953v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We argue that the Transformer revolution is not adequately understood as a merely quantitative expansion of deep learning, but as the emergence of a new paradigm based on a different principle of inference. We interpret the Transformer as a system in which token representations are transformed by parameterized transformations, or transforming concepts. During inference, some of these transformations are dynamically constructed from the current input: previously acquired transformations are first adapted and then applied. At the mechanical-structural level, this dynamic processing is realized through output-weight interconnections, whereby outputs of some networks determine the weights of others. The resulting mode of processing, which we call Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP), provides a framework for explaining strong prompt sensitivity and opens research directions concerning interpretability, control, alternative AI architectures, neuromorphic systems, and possible biological realizations of dynamic processing.

items.title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications
items.content: arXiv:2611.17867v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.
items.author: Astarag Mohapatra
items.summary: This technical report compares fine-tuning recipes for encoder models used as single-pass option selectors (System 1 components), testing four scoring/normalization schemes including one inspired by DeepSeek-V3 expert gates. An UltraBERT-380M encoder beats Qwen3-0.6B on the same training data, with yes-minus-no scoring and sigmoid normalization providing measurable gains. It supports the thesis that small encoders can cheaply replace decoder LLMs for fast routing decisions.
items.reasoning: Single-author empirical recipe comparison with modest scale and narrow benchmarks; useful practical guidance for System 1/2 architectures but limited novelty or rigor.

items.title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
items.content: arXiv:2611.18563v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.

items.summary: The study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model to align space-based radio-frequency vessel detections with AIS trajectories, fusing complementary maritime data sources while modeling noise and timing discrepancies, following the CRISP-DM process. This supports maritime safety and detection of illegal activities where AIS alone is unreliable due to known vulnerabilities.
items.reasoning: A competent domain-specific application of an established probabilistic model (PHMM) to data fusion for maritime monitoring. Methodologically conventional; value lies mainly in the application setting and evaluation on real AIS data.

items.title: NPU-Accelerated GNSS Signal Acquisition
items.content: arXiv:2611.18186v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: On small single-board computers (SBCs), GNSS signal acquisition is a major CPU load. This paper proposes using the neural processing unit (NPU) of an SBC not for machine learning but as an accelerator for the parallel code search in GNSS signal acquisition. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) used in acquisition is decomposed by the four-step DFT into matrix products of small DFTs and expressed by $1\times1$ convolutions, element-wise products, and transposes, which NPUs execute efficiently. Furthermore, we propose a method that divides the DFT, the non-coherent integration, and the peak detection between the CPU and the NPU according to the configuration of the NPU (an NPU with its own memory connected via PCIe, or an NPU sharing memory with the CPU). The proposed method is implemented in the open-source software GNSS receiver Pocket SDR and evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 5 combined with the external AX8850 NPU and on the NPU built into the SoC (RK3588) of the ROCK 5C, a small SBC of comparable size. Compared with acquisition by an optimized CPU implementation, the acquisition of short codes on the Raspberry Pi 5 with the AX8850 is 3.0-3.8 times faster. In the evaluation of the whole receiver, the number of tracking channels that reach their first lock within 30 s with the NPU is 1.5 times that with the CPU, and the time until 90% of the channels are locked is reduced from 66 s to 26 s. Furthermore, because the CPU load of acquisition is reduced, the number of tracking channels that can be processed in real time increases from about 175 to about 230. These results show that using the NPU on SBCs with limited CPU resources is effective for achieving both GNSS signal acquisition and tracking. The implementation is publicly available as open source under the name PocketSDR-NPU.

items.summary: The paper repurposes the neural processing unit of single-board computers as an accelerator for GNSS signal acquisition, expressing the DFT-based code search as operations NPUs execute efficiently. It also proposes CPU-NPU workload division strategies tailored to different NPU memory configurations.
items.reasoning: A creative and practical systems trick of using NPUs for non-ML signal processing, but it is a niche domain contribution without broader AI research significance.

items.title: A late response to "Forecasting is Overrated"
items.content:
Response to Forecasting is Way Overrated, and We Should Stop Funding It

disclaimer

I'm a part-time RA at the Forecasting Research Institute and these are my personal views.

tl;dr

Forecasting platforms backed by EA funders already inform and influence policy-makers on issues of concern to the EA community, and are being used by businesses responsible for managing risk at scale.

However, information consumers can obtain most of the value generated by forecasters without directly interacting with (or paying) the forecasters and forecasting platforms that generate that value.

This missing feedback loop makes it difficult for forecasting organizations to quantify where and how they add value. In the absence of easily quantifiable impact or a clear thematic mandate, the path of least resistance is improving accuracy. Accuracy provides status games for participants, but I view it as a necessary(ish) but not sufficient property for impact.

Beyond accuracy, businesses, governments, and the general public need coverage, latency, explainability, and extensibility with proprietary data sources.

Forecasting organizations, with the exception of organizations focused on forecasting questions of interest to EA funders, should probably dedicate significantly more effort towards solving for these other components of the forecasting supply chain, rather than continuing to optimize for accuracy.

asset managers

Asset managers with roughly $200 billion in combined AUM have cited prediction market and forecasting venue probabilities in their allocation decisions.

A few examples:...

items.title: Wargames inform present policy, not future incident response
items.content:
In January 2024, Ryan Greenblatt and Buck Shlegeris posted "Catching AIs red-handed." This post got on "Best of LessWrong" in 2025, and in December of last year Buck Shlegeris commented on it explaining that he was disappointed it did not lead to more follow-up research. I upvoted the post at the time of the review, and so it seems like it's representative of the analysis the community values.

As it happens, it turned out to be remarkably prescient and near-term-relevant for a theorypost: just this August 2026 we, in fact, got to see what happens when AI companies "catch their AIs red-handed". The parties who wrote the post were, additionally, some of the very people involved in investigating the Hugging Face incident.

I definitely respect these researchers, but I struggle to imagine how this analysis could have been useful. While it seems possible that publishing research like this is what put Redwood in a position to be called upon to investigate in the first place, the piece is just a long and abstract discussion about how (for example) if you catch an AI scheming, it is less likely to succeed (emphasis not mine):

In this post, we’ll discuss a crucial dynamic related to risk from scheming models. Suppose your model is trying to exfiltrate its weights or hack the datacenter or cause some other difficult-to-reverse bad outcome. (We’ll refer to all of these as the model “escaping”, because escape is linguistically convenient and is a good description of many of these difficult-to-reverse bad outcomes.) Our claim: once you’ve caught your models red-handed trying to escape, the situation changes substantially, in ways that are bad for the schemer’s chances of success.

And how, if you catch one of your AIs trying to escape, you should look for other AIs trying to escape:

Proliferation is where you try to capitalize on one example of AIs attempting to escape to find a diverse set of examples of AIs attempting to escape....
items.author: Dean Valentine
items.summary: A LessWrong commentary arguing that theoretical AI-safety writing, exemplified by the 2024 post 'Catching AIs red-handed' by Greenblatt and Shlegeris, offers limited practical value for real incident response. The author contends that when an actual AI-scheming incident occurred at Hugging Face in August 2026, abstract prior analysis did not meaningfully inform the investigation, and that effort should go toward present policy rather than speculative future wargames.

items.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers
items.content: arXiv:2611.17354v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.

items.summary: Compares classical models (SVR, ANN, CNN, LSTM) with quantum-enhanced counterparts for positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN calorimeter benchmark, across three data representations. The study addresses whether representation choice and quantum-classical hybrids add practical value in high-energy physics regression.
items.reasoning: A competent comparative study in a niche application area, but hybrid quantum-classical models on simulated benchmarks remain far from practical advantage, and the machine learning methods themselves are standard. Limited relevance to mainstream AI research.
items.summary_html: Compares classical models (SVR, ANN, CNN, LSTM) with quantum-enhanced counterparts for positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN calorimeter benchmark, across three data representations. The study addresses whether representation choice and quantum-classical hybrids add practical value in high-energy physics regression.
items.content_html: arXiv:2611.17354v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.

items.title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
items.content: arXiv:2611.17846v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.
items.author: Richard J. Young
items.summary: This paper empirically tests whether refusal removal via abliteration has become harder on newer open-weight models, comparing release pairs including Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-4-31B, Olmo-3.1-32B, and Mistral-Small-3.2 against predecessors using direction-based ablation and optimization-based ARA in Heretic 2.0 under matched conditions. It finds refusal removal did not become uniformly harder across five release pairs. The work has dual relevance: it informs both safety researchers studying refusal robustness and documents the ease of jailbreaking open models.

items.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
items.content: arXiv:2611.17583v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs.   In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better.   These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.
items.author: Aleksandr M. Shtraukh-Adamsky, Vladimir M. Adamsky, Irina G. Voloshina, Artemiy D. Spitsyn
items.summary: This theoretical paper exhaustively enumerates all admissible representations and binary action rules in a uniform four-state world to map when representations retaining less information yield higher payoff. It compares constructions under module replacement and per-module optimal action selection across three tasks and four cost tariffs. The results show the informative-pays relationship is non-monotonic and context-dependent.
items.reasoning: A rigorous but very small-scale exact analysis with limited connection to modern ML practice; its value is mainly conceptual for information-theoretic decision theory.

items.title: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
items.content: arXiv:2611.17390v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In generative modeling, standard measure theory adopts the a.e. convention, which legitimately ignores any error component carried by a null-support set: a single null element can hide out-of-domain error inside null support and never be explicitly accounted for. The contribution of this paper is not a new distributional distance, but rather a verifiable structure that writes down which underlying predicate supports a high-level object, when it is invertible, and at which layer the error resides, from which we propose the enumerating posterior-supported prior framework. The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set: the first two layers posit no point elements and take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects; the replica-index counting measure successively discriminates one-to-many collections into injections, lifting object collection from surjection to a quotient-layer bijection; the mutual exclusion of preimages in the shared measure space is resolved by an invertible MPT. Four results consolidate into Thm. 7: binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support via measure descent--recovery, enumerating the morphism itself rather than its preimage and object; their multiplicity is normalized through replica-index injection and accounted as an explicitly first-order error. The contribution of this paper is a transformation from nontrivial-input construction -> engineering-computable first-order output: the binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects, supported via categorical support measure descent--recovery, constitute a substantive nontrivial input---precisely because they lift the out-of-domain error that hid inside null support into a first-order falsifiable coefficient mu_err, a finitely obtainable finite integral first-order error.

items.title: Waveform-based pulse timing enhanced by self-supervised neural regression models for digital nuclear instrumentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.17356v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: With the rapid development of high-sampling-rate digital nuclear devices, their applications in nuclear facilities and related fields become more acceptable, and will possibly become widespread due to the versatility and flexibility of waveform sampling systems. When digitizers reach hundreds of megahertz or gigahertz, their lower limit in time measurement probes into the sub-nanosecond region, expediting their use in a bunch of time-critical scenarios. While conventional algorithms coupled with digital sampling techniques realize fair pulse timing in certain conditions, the potentials are still open to compact and efficient machine learning models. In this paper, we intend to boost the performance of pulse timing with a new paradigm of self-supervised learning on matched waveform pairs. The proposed method combines the mainstream self-supervised loss and the auxiliary weakly-supervised loss on the reference set, jointly improving the timing performance. We apply the method in a gamma/neutron-mixed radiation field, common in nuclear facilities. The simulation and experimental results show that, the proposed method not only outperforms conventional timing algorithms, but also surpasses neural network models based on supervised learning alone. Considering the trained model is lightweight and computationally efficient, it is promising to deploy it on edge devices, like economical microcontrollers with neural processing units.
items.author: Pengcheng Ai, Xiangming Sun
items.summary: This work proposes a self-supervised neural regression paradigm for sub-nanosecond pulse timing in high-sampling-rate digital nuclear instrumentation, where conventional digital algorithms leave performance headroom. The approach aims to be compact and efficient enough for time-critical nuclear facility applications.
items.reasoning: Interesting use of self-supervision to avoid labeled timing data in an instrumentation niche, but the abstract suggests an early-stage method with limited evidence of general AI significance.

items.title: When will AI be better at research taste than you?
items.content:
Some slightly unjustified extrapolations from the AI Futures Project's assumptions.

In their Q3.5 timelines update, they claim that we will get a superhuman AI researcher (one that has better research taste than the best human AI researcher at an AGI company) by 2027. How does that translate to you, the average reader, who is likely not the best AI researcher?

First of all, METR shares their linear extrapolation model, which assumes AI increases at research taste at a constant rate:

From AFP

We start with the recent estimated AECI slope, which is 29 points/year. After that, we have to do some guesswork.

Daniel Kokotajlo estimates that currently, Model 4 has a research taste −3.5 SDs below the median Anthropic researcher, and that AI research taste improves at 3 SDs per year of 2025 AI progress. The AI Futures Project convert this to AECI by dividing 3 SDs with 15 AECI points/year, getting 0.2 SDs per AECI point of improvement. Therefore, 29 points of AECI improvement per year corresponds to 5.8 SDs of improvement per year.

AECI capability improvement, METR

Since SAR is defined elsewhere in the report as +3.09 SDs (equivalent to top 1 in 999), we can simply calculate (3.09 - (-3.5)) / 5.8 = 1.1 years until SAR.

Generated with Claude Opus 5.5. The graph starts from Model 4's estimated release date of September 25th, estimated by the AI Futures Project (read off a graph by Claude).

Under the linear model, interpreted literally:

- October 20, 2026 ( 25 days ago): Claude is better than one Anthropic researcher at research taste
- February 11th, 2027 (89 days later) Claude is better than 10% of Anthropic researchers
- May 3, 2027 (170 days later) Claude is better than half of researchers
- Nov 14, 2027 (exactly a year later!) Claude is better than every Anthropic researcher (SAR)

Replotted with the various models that the AFP uses, the graphs look like this.

items.title: Embryo selection and economic discounting
items.content:
My wife and I are planning to have children soon, and we will be using embryo selection to improve our family’s future well-being. Basically, the idea is that we can take a small sample of cells from each embryo, analyze their DNA, and use the genetic information to help choose which embryos we want to implant.

These days, polygenic scores are good at predicting risk for a lot of diseases, like cancer, heart disease, diabetes, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer’s. And companies like Herasight or Genomic Prediction often give an “embryo health score”[1] that takes an average of the predicted risk for each disease, weighted by how bad each disease is.

But how are those weights calculated? And can we do better?

# Disability-adjusted life years

Diseases are bad in two ways: they can make you die, and they can make your life worse. The “disability-adjusted life year” (DALY) metric captures both of these, by combining years of life lost and years of reduced quality of life (using a factor between 0 and 1 to account for different subjective severity of disease states).[2]

Embryo selection companies, who compute polygenic scores for many different diseases, can add up the DALY burden of all the disease predictions for a given embryo. This gives an overall “embryo health score” that is a composite of these predictions.

DALY scores for five of our embryos, shown against the possible distribution of embryos given the parents’ DNA. Note the left-tailed skew. This is because an increasing genetic risk for a condition causes a nonlinearly increasing risk of having the condition.

### A note on pleiotropy...

The author, writing about their own family planning, explores whether economic discounting assumptions behind those weights can be improved.

However, it is adjacent to core AI research and remains an analytical essay rather than peer-reviewed work with validation.

items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Paper Search: Retrieval Success and Inference Latency on Mac Studio and NVIDIA A100
items.content: arXiv:2611.17929v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Scientific literature search can benefit from locally deployed LLM assistants, which reduce reliance on hosted model providers while giving research teams greater control over their data and infrastructure. This work investigates whether open-weight models can support web-assisted paper retrieval under practical computing constraints. We first characterize inference latency as the input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We then evaluate eight models on the retrieval of 70 papers from seven scientific repositories, using queries that represent three levels of domain knowledge. The results show that retrieval success depends strongly on the selected model and the specificity of the query. And that A100 GPUs are generally faster than the Mac Studio, but its unified memory allows larger models that could not be loaded in the tested GPU configuration.
items.author: Frederic Andriantseheno Rakoto (Mnemosyne), Yannis Bendi-Ouis (Mnemosyne), Xavier Hinaut (Mnemosyne)
items.summary: This work evaluates eight open-weight LLMs on web-assisted scientific paper retrieval across 70 papers from seven repositories, characterizing inference latency on a Mac Studio and dual-A100 server as context grows from 512 to 128k tokens. Retrieval success depends strongly on model choice and query specificity. It offers practical deployment guidance for locally hosted LLM literature-search assistants.
items.reasoning: Useful applied benchmarking with modest scale (70 papers, 8 models) and limited methodological novelty; primarily an engineering evaluation rather than a research contribution.

items.title: Optimizing Drilling Trajectories in Multi-Material Structures Using Quantum Annealers
items.content: arXiv:2611.18121v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this work we present a quantum-hybrid optimization approach for planning drilling trajectories on multi-material structures, with the objective of minimizing total energy consumption. The proposed formulation models the drilling process as a constrained routing problem in which each hole must be visited while accounting for heterogeneous material properties, material-dependent drilling costs and displacement energy, as well as tool-wear penalties. Our method incorporates realistic industrial constraints, including open-path routing and mandatory grouping of holes belonging to the same material to avoid frequent tool-bit changes. The modeled problem is solved using D-Wave's Leap Constrained Quadratic Model Hybrid Solver. To evaluate performance, we benchmark instances ranging from 10 to 55 holes with varying material distributions and cost matrices. The results highlight the capability of quantum-hybrid optimization to handle complex multi-physics constraints and to generate energy-efficient drilling sequences under realistic manufacturing conditions.
items.author: Eneko Osaba, Antonio Rubio-Mateos
items.summary: The paper formulates industrial drilling trajectory planning on multi-material structures as a constrained routing problem with material-dependent costs, tool-wear penalties, and tool-change grouping constraints, solved with D-Wave's Leap hybrid quadratic model solver. It evaluates performance on realistic industrial instances with the goal of minimizing energy consumption.
items.reasoning: An applied quantum-hybrid optimization case study with realistic constraints, but application-focused work of this kind rarely advances AI broadly and quantum annealing advantages remain contested. Solid industrial relevance for the sector but limited novelty.

The modeled problem is solved using D-Wave's Leap Constrained Quadratic Model Hybrid Solver. To evaluate performance, we benchmark instances ranging from 10 to 55 holes with varying material distributions and cost matrices. The results highlight the capability of quantum-hybrid optimization to handle complex multi-physics constraints and to generate energy-efficient drilling sequences under realistic manufacturing conditions.

items.title: Clean Tickets, Wrong Orders: Catching Silent Errors with a Language Model in Your Browser Tab
items.content: arXiv:2611.18284v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A small language model that turns a typed order into structure can fail in two ways. It can print something broken, which any system rejects. Or it can print a clean, well formed order that nobody placed. Our companion work calls the second kind a silent error, and it is the dangerous one. We present a web demo in which a fine-tuned 0.8B parameter model runs entirely inside the visitor's browser tab, through llama.cpp compiled to WebAssembly. No order text leaves the device. The page parses orders as the visitor types, scores every ticket with the PIZZA benchmark's own matcher ported to TypeScript, refuses anything off the menu with "?" so the model can face the open web, and lets visitors hunt for silent errors or try to cause one. Run in the browser on all 1,357 PIZZA test orders, the deployed model writes the same output as the server evaluation for 99.0% of them and reaches the same exact match (0.882); we also report its latency on 3 consumer laptops. Demo: https://wrong.cuyor.com

items.title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Measured Neutron Flux Profiles of the SAFARI-1 Research Reactor
items.content: arXiv:2611.17351v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Knowledge of the neutron flux distribution is essential for safe and effective reactor utilisation. In the SAFARI-1 research reactor, a set of axial flux profiles are periodically measured by activating natural copper wires inserted along the height of the fuel or control assemblies and subsequently measuring their activity using a sodium iodide detector. Improper wire insertion can, however, result in profiles that do not accurately represent the actual neutron flux distribution. Building on previously identified potential indicators of improper wire insertion, an automated approach based on unsupervised learning was developed to detect anomalous axial flux measurements. The measured data were preprocessed using missing-value imputation, decay correction, and normalisation. High-order polynomial fitting was then applied to characterise the axial flux profiles and derive features describing their shape. The Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm was employed to group flux profiles into regular and abnormal clusters based on these features with results matching the known groups. In addition, Convolutional Autoencoders were developed and trained on flux profiles from central and peripheral core positions to identify deviations from the regular profiles through reconstruction error, achieving better performance in central assemblies than in peripheral assemblies. The developed framework is intended to provide feedback to reactor operation by identifying potential wire-insertion problems in the manual technique used for axial flux monitoring at SAFARI-1.

items.title: Poetry 'resurrection' from LLMs
items.content: arXiv:2611.17464v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In an era where linguistic creativity is challenged by algorithmic authorship, we pose a provocative question: can artificial intelligence (AI) write an infinite poem? We set up two experiments to investigate the quantitative and qualitative output produced by AI utilizing couplets that evidence a poetic relationship between end words, the only variation in a strict anaphoric, litany structure. Our results show that while AI can generate interesting pairings, it still falls short of human-level creativity and understanding of poetic relationships. We offer commentary and a brief survey of the field of computational poetry experiments, tracing back authorial intention and distinctions of 'natural' and 'artificial' poetry, as well as justifying why couplet form is suited to testing AI's poetic output. Experiment 1 relies on manual prompting and co-creation to extend the original poem, which is developed into an animated webpage installation and interactive artwork. Experiment 2 reliably achieves automated output reaching the 1000 benchmark via an alternative method of using an LLM in combination with semantic similarity, of which Method 2 demonstrates a higher capacity for semantic and quantitative poetic output. These experiments highlight the limitations of current LLMs' generation capacity at the word level but also suggest that poetry will also respond and revive by incorporating AI workflows.

The paper also surveys computational poetry and discusses authorial intention in natural versus artificial poetry.

items.title: Toward On-Device Markerless 6DoF Tracking of a Physical Manipulative on a Mixed-Reality Headset: A Preliminary Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.18438v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: AR-Classroom uses physical models and virtual overlays to help learners explore spatial transformations. To align these overlays on a standalone headset, we developed a markerless six-degree-of-freedom(6DoF) tracker for a LEGO airplane on the Meta Quest 3. A compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders predicts 20 keypoints from dynamic RGB crops resized to 128 by 128 pixels. A perspective-n-point solver estimates the airplane's pose from these predictions and the corresponding 3D landmarks. In a paired evaluation on 1,000 synthetic validation images, cropping guided by ground-truth boxes increased the detection rate on annotated images from 32.5 to 46.2 percent. Mean keypoint F1 increased from 42.9 to 44.6 percent, with lower keypoint precision in the cropped view. In preliminary headset tests, 2 Hz was the highest tested tracking target at which the application maintained approximately 72 frames per second. A headset demonstration illustrates virtual overlay alignment with the physical airplane before and after a manual rotation. Quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage will be measured in future work.

items.summary: A preliminary system for markerless 6DoF tracking of a LEGO airplane on Meta Quest 3 for AR education, using a compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders to predict 20 keypoints feeding a perspective-n-point pose solver. Detection rates on synthetic validation remain modest (roughly 32-46 percent depending on cropping), reflecting early-stage results.
