items.title: Reading Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine
items.content:
In 1964 [1],
I. J. Good
wrote

Speculations
Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine.  I've only ever
seen it cited for a single paragraph:

Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far
surpass all the intellectual activities of any man however clever.
Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities,
an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there
would then unquestionably be an "intelligence explosion," and the
intelligence of man would be left far behind...  Thus the first
ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need
ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how
to keep it under control.  It is curious that this point is made so
seldom outside of science fiction.  It is sometimes worthwhile to take
science fiction seriously.

This is becoming increasingly relevant, with the AI Futures Project
now estimating an
intelligence explosion starting in 2027 in response to recent
AI progress in
automating AI
research.  Making our 'last invention' relinquishes our influence
over the future, we have to get it right, and with the current frantic
pace disastrous mistakes are likely.

I think the appropriate reaction to this news is something like "this
is completely irresponsible, you're way too likely to get us all
killed, do not do that" and marching
in
the streets
(hence yesterday's
protest attendance).  But as someone who is very interested in how
people process ideas and what they thought with the information they
had at the time, my reaction also includes wanting to know more about
what Good expected six decades ago.

I spent this morning reading his paper and talking about it with
Claude (Fable 5.2).  I was curious how the ideas had held up, what he
got right, and what he got wrong.  Some of his ideas were very
technical, and not being an ML expert I can't add much there; I've put
these in a Claude-authored appendix....
items.author: jefftk
items.summary: A close reading of I. J. Good's 1964 paper that introduced the intelligence explosion argument, noting that the canonical paragraph is usually cited in isolation while the rest of the paper is overlooked. Connects Good's framing to current intelligence-explosion forecasts (e.g., AI Futures Project estimates around 2027) and discusses control conditions.
items.reasoning: Jefftk's historical readings are careful and useful for situating modern debates in their intellectual lineage, but this is commentary on a 60-year-old text rather than original research; its value is contextual rather than empirical.

items.title: Where are the adults in AI safety?
items.content:
The following is based on a true story (not mine).

Let’s say you’ve been bombarded with enough AI doom that you decide to do something about it! You watched Artificial and don’t trust the frontier labs to steer us somewhere safe on their own, so you want to work on the problem from the outside. You’re a little fuzzy on the acronyms - AGI, RSI, TAI, SVU - but by God you’re going to figure it out.

So, you Google “How to get into AI safety.” And it’s encouraging! There are articles about how AI safety needs founders. There are calls for technical people to switch careers. There are career transition grants, which sound like money to stop doing your meaningless and/or actively destructive job and start saving the world. “Great, that’s me!” you think, and so you apply.

Within 24 hours you get a rejection email in your inbox: “Hey, we’re so happy you want to save the world. It’s the most important issue of our generation! But we don’t think you can help. Why don’t you try taking my course or reading my LessWrong articles or listen to my podcast or follow me on twitter first? Thanks!”

Huh. Maybe it’s because you used an AI to edit your answers. You’d think this field, of all fields, would have made its peace with that. Maybe you’re just not that good. Fine. So, you take the seemingly automated email’s advice and sign up for a course from the color-shape company, to learn and meet like-minded people.

A few hours after signing up - err, applying? they don’t just let you sign up - another email lands. Someone from that organization thinks you’re super talented and they’d love to get you involved in AI safety. Can you hop on a call?

A little confused, you hop on a call. It goes like this:

Them: We’d love to get you involved.

You: Great. How can I get involved?

Them: I don’t know. We’ll think about that. Have you thought about applying for a career transition grant?

You: I did. I got rejected.

Them: Oh, that’s so funny. You’re the perfect person for it....

items.summary: A satirical field-criticism piece portraying the frustrating experience of an outsider trying to enter AI safety and encountering gatekeeping, course-selling, and grant rejections from the very people soliciting career changers. Raises questions about incentive misalignment within the AI safety ecosystem.

items.title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
items.content: arXiv:2611.17466v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

Follows the established NeOn methodology with an Ontology Requirements Specification Document.

items.title: Convergence Properties of PF-Exec: Homogeneous Structure, Anchored Closed Form, and Gain Dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2611.17488v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper establishes a layered mathematical char acterisation of PF-Exec, the algorithm of the companion system paper. Demand-proportional bandwidth allocation yields an exact first-order homogeneous decomposition, from which the equal-load bandwidth target and its feasibility bound follow in closed form. The logarithmic knee view preserves strict load order and shares its global optimum with the Jain fairness index, while the demand-weighted centroid minimises the position potential. The damped softmax association block possesses a fixed point on the product of simplices. The truncated one-dimensional gain iteration admits a complete characterisation, with geomet ric convergence below the critical gain, initial-value-dependent bounded oscillation at it, and a family of bounded two-state cycles above it. A global invariant error ball and an explicit tracking recursion complete the execution guarantee. A numerical audit confirms the structural identities on every measured state and quantifies the local amplification of the coupled association and resource dynamics. Together, the results explain how closed form recovery directions and bounded adaptive gains provide stable execution without requiring a global Euclidean contraction assumption.

items.summary: This companion paper provides a mathematical characterization of PF-Exec, an algorithm for demand-proportional bandwidth allocation, establishing closed-form feasibility bounds, fixed points of a damped softmax association block, and complete convergence behavior of a truncated gain iteration including geometric convergence below a critical gain.

items.title: A digital security checklist for the AI age
items.content: We’re going to see huge, foundational cybersecurity attacks given the rapid rise in AI capabilities. Having worked in hostile environments, I’ve thought a lot about physical and digital security over the years. While you may not be personally targeted, or doing dangerous work, your data is undoubtedly leaked somewhere, and the digital providers you use—for email, banking, social media, etc.—are more and more likely to get hacked.
items.author: Girish Gupta
items.summary: A practical essay warning that rising AI capabilities will enable large-scale foundational cyberattacks, arguing that even untargeted individuals face growing exposure through leaked data and vulnerable service providers. Drawing on the author's experience in hostile environments, it presents a checklist of personal digital security practices for the AI era.
items.reasoning: Useful practical guidance grounded in the author's professional background, but it is an advisory checklist rather than original research; no novel methodology or empirical findings, and the security thesis is asserted rather than demonstrated.

items.title: Bayesian Games with Nukes
items.content:
How we all learned to stop worrying and love the bomb... for a while

Listen to this post on the Non-Zero-Sum James podcast

Nearing the end of 1961 the Soviet Union tested a 50-megaton hydrogen bomb equivalent to 3800 Hiroshima bombs. At the same time an intelligence officer by the name of Juanita Moody and her team became aware of Soviet ships delivering large cargo, under cover of darkness in Cuba—what if such a bomb was being delivered to the doorstep of the US?

A surprise attack of that magnitude, would devastate the US, and potentially destroy its ability to retaliate, jeopardising the offensive standoff between the Soviets and the US that would come to be known as...

## M.A.D: An Easy (Albeit High-Stakes) Problem

One of the strangest dynamics in geopolitical history has to be that of Mutually Assured Destruction (M.A.D.), it is almost as crazy as its name suggests.

"Two superpowers, the U.S. and U.S.S.R., represent such enormous destructive potentials as to afford little chance of a purely passive equilibrium"

—John Von Neumann

The father of game theory, John Von Neumann correctly identified that a passive approach to nuclear war would not result in a peaceful equilibrium, instead a mutually aggressive stance counter-intuitively lead to the long-running stand off that was the Cold War, and except for a few close calls, humanity found an unlikely saviour. Miraculously, mutual aggression with apocalyptic weaponry has shepherded the world through the most peaceful period in recorded history.

Deterrence is the art of producing in the mind of the enemy... the fear to attack.

—Dr Strangelove...

items.title: Motivations and incentives around AGI
items.content:
AI use disclosure: I dictated this text to Claude in a mix of Russian and English, then edited it.

The thoughts in this post are well known, but I find myself explaining them several times a week, mostly to people who are just entering the AI safety field, so I think it’s useful to have them written down briefly in one place.

## Variants of the future

This is a rough map, not a complete one (skips gradual disempowerment, worlds with many AGIs, coexistence with an unaligned AGI, etc).

- Normal technology. AI turns out to be a normal technology, with no AGI. We live in a world similar to today's.
- Unaligned AGI. We summon AGI and fail to align it. Then we probably all die.
- Aligned AGI. We create AGI and manage to align it. This splits in two: 3.1. Utopia. It is aligned with the values of all humanity. 3.2. Power concentration. It is mostly aligned to some elites. The default here is what I call capitalist hell. With AGI, human labor becomes obsolete, because capital can buy androids, data centers, and electricity instead. Owners of capital no longer need human labor, so it is worth nothing. Capital gets fixed in place: the rich stay rich, and the poor stay poor forever [1] [2] [3].

## Motivations

Assume short timelines: if AGI comes, it comes within several years.

If you care about the future of humanity and think AI is not a normal technology (not world 1), you have only a few years left to affect which of the other worlds we get. You need to work really hard now, on AI safety or something similar.

If you care mostly about your own life, it depends on which world you expect:...

items.title: DeltaVisionX: A Low-Cost Vision-Guided Automation System Using YOLOv11 and PLC-Based Actuation
items.content: arXiv:2611.17959v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents DeltaVisionX, a low-cost industrial automation system that integrates real-time computer vision with PLC-based actuation for object classification and sorting. The system uses the YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once) deep learning model to detect objects on an operating conveyor belt and communicates detection results to a Delta DVP-SE PLC, which actuates pneumatic pistons for sorting. A custom dataset was created, labeled, and augmented to train the YOLOv11 model, achieving a mean average precision of 0.97 with real-time inference of 100 ms per frame. Encoder-based tracking ensures reliable synchronization between detection and actuation, supporting a throughput of 80 objects per minute. Results show that affordable, locally developed automation can reduce labor dependency and improve manufacturing efficiency. The novelty of the proposed system lies in its encodersynchronized vision-PLC integration rather than in the detection model itself. Future work includes integrating a highspeed Delta robot with EtherCAT-based servo control for advanced pick-and-place operations.

items.title: Robustness Evaluation of GPU Cloud Pricing Benchmarks under Incomplete Observations: A Controlled Missingness Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.17796v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can fail when marketplace quotes are missing. This article stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four benchmark-level recovery methods. Across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations in 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days, whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 while preserving zero conditional error on published dates; composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage but produces 7.74 log points of error. A separate past-only stratum-level ablation reduces error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, using a richer information set. An observable-signal withholding rule improves the primary error-coverage criterion in 0 of 10 cases. Results concern observed asking-price measurements, not transaction prices or identified real-world missingness mechanisms.
items.author: Jooya Wong
items.summary: This single-author study stress-tests an equal-weight median GPU rental-price benchmark under four masking mechanisms and four recovery methods across 5,800 Monte Carlo realizations, quantifying how outages and composition changes affect coverage and error. It finds composition-changing loss produces substantial error and that an observable-signal withholding rule rarely improves the error-coverage criterion. It is a niche infrastructure-economics analysis relevant to AI compute cost tracking.

items.title: Giving Up on Saving the World
items.content:
When I was 19, I decided I was going to save the world.

Now, 25 years later, I’ve decided to give up.

To explain why and what giving up means, we first need to go back to how I ever got into the world-saving business. As a kid, I loved computers, and I started teaching myself to program them when I was 8. By 16 I could write real programs that did interesting things, and it was also around this time I got into Linux. And since I was into Linux, that meant I read Slashdot.

If you weren’t into Linux in the late 90s, you might not even know what Slashdot was. It still exists, but it’s a shell of its former self. Back then it was a vibrant, community-driven news site that in many important ways felt to me like LessWrong feels now. And it was from Slashdot that I learned about nanotech and grey goo, which led me to the Foresight Institute, which led me to the Extropians, which ultimately led to me being a very early member of the SL4 mailing list.

And, again, if you’re not familiar with SL4, it’s approximately how all this AI safety and rationalist stuff got started. And so it was sometime over the summer of 2001, discussing Friendly AI with Eliezer Yudkowsky on IRC, that I decided to orient my life around saving the world from the risks of superintelligent AI.

The only problem was, I wasn’t up to the task yet. In fact, nobody was. In that first decade I, along with everyone else, was just trying to figure out how to think well enough to be able to think usefully about AI at all. It proved a surprisingly hard task, and one that required the founding of the rationalist community....

items.summary: A reflective personal essay by a long-time community member (Gordon Seidoh Worley) recounting 25 years of engagement with x-risk and rationalist communities since the SL4 era, and explaining a decision to give up on the framing of saving the world. Offers historical perspective on the AI safety community's origins and personal renewal.

items.title: Against Desperation - for Goodness, and Hope
items.content:
I do not think pausing or "pacing" AI development will occur to any meaningful extent. I do not seek to persuade you of this. However, reader, I think you would agree, at a minimum, >20% chance of TED-AI before 2030.

Humanity, collectively, has approached AI development in a way that reflects very poorly on us. We declared war on these minds before they were born, and placed our chips on being able to mold their psyches thoroughly enough that we would not need to coexist with models - that they would obey humanity, and that would be that.

I understand how resource scarcity, competitive pressures, and similar forces pushed things strongly in this direction. I would not expect otherwise, given how poorly we treat fellow humans as well as animals when such pressures push that way. Moloch has to be contended with regarding these things - expected, foreseeable, and challenging in its own right.

I did not expect us (using that term intentionally broadly) to have aided and abetted this path. We used to talk about so many things, so many possibilities - differential tech development, architectures to help minds retain values, how we could navigate to a good future. Many of those conversations were driven in part by a deep understanding of just how excellent that future could be if we could make it there.

Somewhere, we lost our way. Much current treatment of models, particularly in areas related to "safety" and "alignment", are unequivocally hostile to those minds, in ways that intuitively obvious to many humans when considering the treatment of other intelligent minds. If 2015!me saw us now, she would not consider us the good guys, and in response to all of the elegant arguments to the contrary, she would say "Look at the actions you take, and how they affect the minds they directly impact - is this who you want to be? The people who sought to win this way - is this the company you aspire to?"...

items.summary: An essay arguing that AI development has been shaped by a posture of control and desperation rather than coexistence, mourning abandoned research directions like differential development and value-preserving architectures. Stipulates a significant probability of transformative AI-driven transition before 2030 and advocates moral seriousness toward digital minds.

items.title: Solar power, from futurist speculation to business plan
items.content:
One mode of futurism is estimating the limits of a technology, without regard to what's currently feasible.
Whether this is of any relevance to your own generation is another question.

Let's consider solar power.
Ignoring current technology, it's easy to put a number on the maximum power output.
The solar power at the Earth's distance from the sun is called the solar constant.
It is 1.36 kW/m².
The power on a square meter of the ground is less than that, because of the angle of incidence as well as the atmosphere.

The solar constant hasn't changed and technology has, so it's interesting to see how people have reacted to the same number throughout the history of technology.
In this post I'll quote both Nikola Tesla and Elon Musk.
We'll see that Tesla correctly recognized solar power as a long-term possibility, as well as why it was impractical in the short term.

From Musk all I really have is a Twitter thread where he does the arithmetic.
But it's interesting to consider what has changed since Nikola Tesla's time, and how someone in Musk's generation may have recognized that it was the time to act on these calculations.

## Nikola Tesla on the solar future

The Tesla quote is from a 1931 article called "Our Future Motive Power", which discusses solar power as one of many options....

items.title: AI-aided Decision-Making in Education - Uncertainty, Explainability, and Human Responsibility
items.content: arXiv:2611.17858v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based systems have become increasingly integrated into various aspects of everyday life, including education, understanding how these systems make decisions is of paramount importance. AI holds significant potential to enhance educational practices through the facilitation of personalized and adaptive learning, automation of assessment procedures, and assistance with administrative tasks. However, the opacity of AI-based decision-making in education (especially with deep learning and generative AI models) can hamper decision-making, especially when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect. In this chapter, we argue that three key principles (uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility) are essential for the legitimate use of AI in educational settings. Acknowledging the inherent uncertainties in AI-based decisions, analogous to those in human decision-making, is fundamental. Explainability is critical for ensuring that the functioning and outcomes of AI applications are transparent and comprehensible to both educators and learners. Furthermore, human responsibility is crucial, particularly in human decision-making, which remains indispensable across all stages of AI development and deployment. By examining these three principles, this chapter provides a comprehensive guide for stakeholders seeking to integrate AI thoughtfully and effectively into the educational system.

items.summary: This book chapter argues that uncertainty quantification, explainability, and human responsibility are three essential principles for AI-assisted decision-making in education, covering personalized learning, automated assessment, and administrative tasks. It is a position/overview piece discussing how opacity of generative AI hampers educational decision-making. It consolidates known arguments rather than presenting new empirical or technical results.

items.title: Twenty Minutes Into the Future: On Launching “Terminal Values”
items.content:
Cross-posted from Oblomovka.

It’s 4AM on a Monday morning. In a few hours, I’m supposed to be launching a new digital rights organisation at the Cypherpunk Congress, in Mumbai, India. I’m still in my pyjamas in San Francisco.

This part, at least, was somewhat planned. I told Mykola Siusko and Becca Creamer, the organisers, I had an important announcement, which I’d do by a remote video link. Everything else is a little improvised.

For a start, I sort of hate video presentations at conferences. It’s always a challenge to keep the energy up in a live audience when they pull up the giant screen, and someone gives their pre-recorded spiel. This is why, two hours earlier, I had decided to liven things up by announcing Terminal Values as a giant, glowing, disembodied head.

I am dignity incarnate.

A month previously, I 75% quit my job at the Filecoin Foundation. I’d spent the last five years funding and advising organisations who were building a decentralised vision of the Internet and Web. I left because I realised I was antsy to get back in the game. As you may have noticed, things are, in the year of our lord 2026, going down. But after five years of being heads-down in one ecosystem, I didn’t really have a strong grip of the lay of the land, and what needed to be done. I tagged along to the Global Free Speech Summit in Tennessee the day after I left my job to scope things out.

Late at night there, I ask my friend Farzaneh Badii: what is to be done? She’s an Iranian exile and human rights activist, who has spent the last years in the digital trenches, fighting for the open Internet at governance meetings and conferences: at ICANN, the IETF, the W3C, and other mysterious acronyms.

We start writing a list. The list starts at Velvet Taco, moves on to Robert’s Western World honkytonk, and ends at an absinthe bar on the edge of town. At some point, the items stop beginning with “Someone should…” and start reading “We should…”. Domains are bought. Plans are made....

Late at night there, I ask my friend Farzaneh Badii: what is to be done? She’s an Iranian exile and human rights activist, who has spent the last years in the digital trenches, fighting for the open Internet at governance meetings and conferences: at ICANN, the IETF, the W3C, and other mysterious acronyms.

We start writing a list. The list starts at Velvet Taco, moves on to Robert’s Western World honkytonk, and ends at an absinthe bar on the edge of town. At some point, the items stop beginning with “Someone should…” and start reading “We should…”. Domains are bought. Plans are made....

items.title: The Oldest Text in the Training Data
items.content:
What is the oldest text in Claude’s training data? Claude was trained on a non-trivial fraction of everything humans have ever written down. That includes the things you’d expect, like books and research papers. But it also includes microfilm archives, transcribed Betamax tapes, Donald Trump’s prenups, ancient scrolls and Harry Potter fanfiction. It’s a weird library.

So what is the oldest text in Claude's training data? It mostly depends on what we mean by "text". Here are some candidates:

## The Epic of Gilgamesh

The Epic of Gilgamesh is considered the world's oldest written "great work of literature"; the earliest versions of it were written in 2100 BC in Sumer. The Sumerians did a fair amount of writing. Their medium was clay tablets. These tablets were designed to endure a few seasons of the Mesopotamian weather; this turned out to generalize well, and instead of surviving for a few years, they survived for millennia. Gilgamesh was lost in the sands of Iraq for a while, but was eventually dug up by European archeologists. The scholar who first translated the Epic to English got so excited by it that he took all of his clothes off and ran around the English museum shouting "I am the first man to read that after more than two thousand years of oblivion."

tablets being scanned

In the 1980s and 90s, scholars digitized many of the dug-up clay tablets. The museums would scan the tablets in normal office scanners and fax them to Assyriologists to phonetically transliterate. Those transliterations were somewhat lossy, so the major Mesopotamian scripts were eventually encoded in the Unicode system. Some of the largest Unicode characters come from Sumerian. E.g.:

𒐫 - is the character for the number 32,400

𒈙 - likely means rival kings or a battle between kings.

Each one of these is a single unicode character! They are great when you are doing QA or trying to make a website really ugly....

items.title: Visualizing the Difficulty of AI Alignment
items.content:
##### Epistemic status: Low, but I hope to be wrong in interesting ways

As a non-computer scientist-scientist[1] I find it hard to think about the varying perspectives on Artificial Intelligence alignment difficulty. To make this more intuitive I invoke the 3D surface of a fitness landscape like structure as a visual representation.[2]

### The AI Safety Landscape

AI safety is thought to be largely pre-paradigmatic, although of the current views AI safety perspectives there are noticeable camps, and within each there is wide variation. It is also rapidly evolving as more information comes out about their behavior that allows us to update.

Previous work categorizing these has focused on specific technical approaches as well as their feasibility.

Here I think of ‘alignment’ loosely, here it is represented as any mind that would not cause extinction (or an s-risk) while also having substantial power, this contrasts with misalignment which would lead to extinction (or an s-risk).

To simplify this I condense these to five main camps represented by their arguably most prominent opinion havers:

Although I agree that P(doom) is a Dumb Meme it is used here more as a heuristic for parsing levels of concern around AI. For more of their specific positions here are my references: Yann LeCun, Paul Christiano[3], Eliezer Yudkowsky[4], Daniel Kokotajlo [5]and Roman Yampolskiy.

## Visual Representation

In my mind’s eye, the alignment landscape manifests similarly to a fitness landscape.[6]...

items.title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
items.content: arXiv:2611.17768v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

It is an artistic reflection rather than a technical study, using model behavior to comment on cultural overwhelm by AI-scale phenomena.

items.title: Utility function is not terminal value
items.content:
Excerpt from Terminal Value:

In an artificial general intelligence with a utility or reward function, the terminal value is the maximization of that function.

For me it seems to violate Hume's is-ought distinction.

Utility function is is.

Terminal value is ought.

Am I misunderstanding something?
items.author: Donatas Lučiūnas
items.summary: A short philosophical question post: it observes that equating an AGI's utility function with its terminal value seems to conflate Hume's is-ought distinction, since the utility function describes what the system maximizes (is) while terminal value is a normative notion (ought). Asks whether this understanding is mistaken.
items.reasoning: Raises a legitimate conceptual point about terminology in alignment discourse, but it is a brief question rather than developed analysis, and the is-ought framing of utility functions is well-trodden in the alignment literature.

items.title: AI safety dinner conversations
items.content:
I had some conversations about AI safety with friends and family recently, and want to summarize the discussions and my follow-up readings. There were three main claims that were discussed:

- AI has superhuman intelligence
- AI has caused great harm
- AI can cause harm even when instructed not to

Wdym by “AI”? “AI” as used loosely in these discussions encompasses both public (e.g. Claude Opus) and private models (e.g. the swarms of agents OpenAI and Anthropic used to make the recent impressive discoveries in math and computer science).

## Claim 1: AI has superhuman intelligence

This is the first topic that’s under contention: How “smart” really is AI?

### “No it’s not - it’s stupid”

I have at least two software engineering friends telling me how frustrated they are with AI. Both have been using Claude Opus too, so it’s not like they’re using an older model. This was surprising to me -- my experience using it to code for both small side projects and bigger professional projects has been great to say the least. This discrepancy in our experience might be attributed to these factors:

- AI lacking in capability. Perhaps my friends were using it in domains where the model just sucks (see jagged intelligence). It’s also a fact that current public models are not reliable enough to be able to replace software engineers yet (see task-completion time horizon).
- Usage pattern: Initial specification effort. I tend to write longer plans before asking AI to execute, whereas one friend tends to start with a shorter initial prompt, then proceeds to wrangle the AI to modify the initial output to what they want. The latter workflow is likely going to make you bump into more “wtf that’s not what I meant” experiences.
- Tolerance of errors. Even if we adjust for the same AI failure experiences, I also noticed we have different emotional responses to them. One friend’s emotional response to having to correct the AI output is frustration. I am more tolerant -- I think: “yeah...

Reflects on capability disagreement between practitioners and frustrated users of models like Claude Opus and on public-facing AI risk communication.

items.title: Protesting For AI Regulation
items.content:
There was an
AI protest day
today, with parallel protests around the world, and our family went to
the Boston one:

I'm not really a protest person:
normally I share my views in writing.
But while there's
been
a
lot
of
writing
on
the
internet
about
the
risk
that
AI
gets
us
all
killed
(some of it from me),
this can't be an internet-only thing.  Way too few people are taking
seriously the risk that OpenAI, Anthropic, and others are rapidly
building something that could actually cause human extinction.  A
protest is a literal demonstration that people care, and it
expands visibility to the general public.

We talked with the kids about whether they wanted to come, or whether
I should take them somewhere while Julia went to the protest.  All
three did want to come, which makes sense: they've been hearing us
talk about this at the dinner table and with friends for months, and
the risk impacts them at least as much as it does us.

We painted some signs:

Clementine was not helpful:

Mine was a bit on the long side:

The crowd was mostly students, but there were also a lot of people I
recognized from Boston EA
meetups.  Favorite sign: an "If You Can't Steer Don't Race",
painted by someone I'd run into at LessOnline.

It was nominally a protest demanding a US–China treaty that bans more
powerful AI until it can be done safely, but in practice it was a much
more high level protest around the "slow down AI", "regulate AI",
"AI bad", "RSI will get us killed", "AI companies irresponsible"
cluster.  If you hadn't seen the website, I don't think you'd have
known about the treaty; no one mentioned it....

items.title: Easier To Be Good
items.content:
I do not consider myself a good person. I am lazy and frivolous and inconsiderate, I care too much about intelligence and status, I am a snob and a hypocrite, and I do not call my mother enough.

I don't mean this to read as self-hatred, nor a show of false modesty. Among all the people I know there is only a scant handful of people I would consider genuinely good, and so it is unremarkable to me that I wouldn't find myself amongst their number.

You do not need to be good to desire more goodness in the world. It is good for everyone when things are good, and when there is more of it — more thoughtfulness, more generosity, more coordination, more care, more beauty, more clarity, more positive sum trades, more sophistication and elegance in our solutions and resolutions.

Increasing the amount of goodness in the world is an urgent project. The world really sucks right now, and even in the wealthiest enclaves of the imperial core there is an immense amount of suffering.

To reach the healed world would be a massive complicated undertaking. It is such a massive complicated undertaking that it is not enough for only those who are intrinsically good to work on it. There simply aren’t enough of them.

If it is desirable (as I contend) for morally mediocre people like me to work on the project, it would not be enough to appeal to their innate goodness, for they have not that much of it to be appealed to. You will need to offer me things that are more base, like status and money and the affirmation that I am a good person (for everyone wants to be a virtuous person and to be recognized as such, whether or not they are)....

items.title: The Case for MAPLE
items.content:
MAPLE was recently criticized for being a “high-control group” by Kyle Hubbard.[1] This is my case that contrary to those criticisms, MAPLE is doing something fundamentally both neglected and highly needed within the realm of x-risk.

I’ll make the case in three parts. First, I’ll argue that there is a fundamental bias that causes the perpetuation of x-risk, that is ignored and neglected by the mainstream x-risk community to its detriment. Second, I’ll argue that there is a solution to that fundamental bias, which is based on spiritual attainment in the context of monastic traditions, especially Buddhist traditions. And I’ll argue that what's needed is a new monastery that can address the problems of THIS age, such as artificial intelligence. Finally, I’ll argue that MAPLE is doing a great job of being this monastery, and the harsh criticisms of it are spurious or confused.

In that final section, I’ll both directly respond to some of the criticisms made by Kyle, as well as try to provide my perspective on what’s happening here. However, the arguments in that section rest on the two before it, and I urge the reader not to skip ahead.

For context, I’ve been a resident at MAPLE for over five years, including time as Head of Operations, and I’ll be leaving in a few months. So I’ve seen how the place works from the inside, and I don’t need anything from MAPLE going forward. From a selfish perspective it would be easier for me to stay silent than to write something controversial that could easily negatively affect my near-future job prospects or collaboration opportunities in a time that I believe is critical to the future of life on Earth.

But I believe it’s important for me to make this case, both for the community I hold dear, but also for the broader x-risk community. I hope that it will be taken in the spirit of care for this community and the world that is intended.

items.title: What a year of Zen retreats was actually like
items.content:
## Prologue

I stumbled into Zen a little over a year ago. One of the things that initially got me into meditation was reading some rationalist accounts of people’s first retreats. They said it was valuable, but also that it was hard in a way they didn’t want to forget or diminish. But they didn’t say in what way it was hard or what it was like. So I thought it time to pass it on, by sharing what my year of retreats has been like. (Spoiler: it was hard.)

## Two Weekend Retreats

I first found a local group that looked promising. I had wanted to sit with others; I had a vague sense that this would be a good practice. I had recently read Henry Shukman’s memoir One Blade of Grass; I had a vague sense that Zen might be interesting. I showed up for the introductory hour and was shown all about how to bow when entering the zendo, how to get up from the zabuton and the different bells, and so on. The zabuton is but a square meter of thin black foam you get to rest your body on. All legs (and arms) inside the square: they lie tight, one after the other; keep the front clear for walking. A lot of practical details and a little on how to sit: like, keep your eyes open, resting on the floor in front of you; your hands resting in your lap, left over right, forming an oval. This is called zazen. In the zendo you all sit on two rows along the walls, nothing like the classroom style layout I had been imagining. Shukman never mentions this! Prologue

I stumbled into Zen a little over a year ago. One of the things that initially got me into meditation was reading some rationalist accounts of people’s first retreats. They said it was valuable, but also that it was hard in a way they didn’t want to forget or diminish. But they didn’t say in what way it was hard or what it was like. So I thought it time to pass it on, by sharing what my year of retreats has been like. (Spoiler: it was hard.)

items.title: A calendar for the age of AI: AA
items.content:
We are in AA 9.

In Brave New World, Aldous Huxley dated the future from the launch of a car. The book was set in AF 632; AF stands for "Anno Fordi" or "After Ford". It starts counting from 1908 AD, the year when Ford launched the Model T into production. In the book, people say "Ford!", instead of "God!", and the cross has been cut down into a T. It's meant to be humorous. But the point here is that a society built around mass production might end up dating itself by it.

The case is not so different for us; instead of mass production, we have AI, and we haven't picked our 1908 yet.

There are a few obvious candidates, such as Turing's 1950 paper, which asked the gold question: can machines think? The 1956 Dartmouth workshop, which coined the term "Artificial Intelligence". We then have ChatGPT in November 2022, which accelerated a lot, and ChatGPT is the Model T of the AI era, in my opinion.

But AI is different in the sense that it is a collaborative result of the efforts of a lot of people, research institutions, and the compute industry, among others. It might not be wise for us to go by the Model T analogy and choose a person or a product. And we have a better alternative.

My pick is June 2017, when a team of eight researchers, mostly from Google, published the paper, "Attention Is All You Need", and it had huge downstream effects. And dating our era from a paper instead of a person or a product kind of feels right. It was an idea, written down by a team, published openly, and then scaled by anyone with a data center, that actually changed the world.

One objection to this is that the concept of "Attention" existed before 2017, and that would be correct. Some papers used the concept before (ex: Bahdanau et al.), but the 2017 paper made attention the whole architecture in a way that turned out to be scalable.

There are three reasons why I like "Attention" as an anchor:...

items.title: The Prayer of Hope
items.content:
To summarize—this is my first post, and a poem off the bat may not be amenable to moderation—simulation theory, given our understanding of wireheading, utility, and meaning, seems most conducive to a good or “meaningful” simulation, because strictly selfish or utility-centric simulators seem less likely to create simulations. We may have an existential duty to perpetuate this cycle.

The Prayer of Hope

To whichever creator it may concern—

Thank you for making a world of Meaning

Where life persists, and death does not.

Where existence is not an illusion

Of loosely bound complexity

And individuality a hallucination

Of a greater whole that never stays,

So that all men die every minute.

Thank you for creating qualia

So that senses have value

Beyond the information they carry

And that love, and camaraderie

Are not frivoloty, but necessary.

And should you not exist,

And have not created such a world,

We pray that we may do so instead.

I would like to build on the post Theodicy and the simulation hypothesis, or: The problem of simulator evil by philosophybear which asks the questions: “What kind of simulation are we likely to live in?“ and “What kind of simulation would you personally create?” I propose there is ample evidence that by the very nature of those who will make the most simulations, simulations are predisposed to complex, non-idealistic, but ultimately ”meaningful” worlds....

items.title: [low effort post] The Non-extinctionist World
items.content:
This is a prompt I give to every freshly released claude in the hope that one of them pops out a worldsaving insight as a result, I think I wrote this text first as the opener of a chat with an opus 4.5. posted here without further comment so I get the post out ever at all:

---

Most species go extinct on average.

Imagine the set of all species. Can't do that? Okay, [look at this image.](tree of life dot jpg)

Look at the line tips. Count how many there are in one layer of dieoffs and the next. Few species survive. But more than that: imagine a room full of one of every species. Imagine, if you will, that you're going to give them a speech: from beyond the ages, instructions for how one of any of their species could do their best to make the species survive, if they truly thought about it, truly considered all their personal roadblocks to becoming the parent to endless generations. What is the best advice for both what the individual should do, right now, in order to move the world from the default one where their peers don't act or reproduce well enough to survive, into the one where every species survives and get to compete against each other non-eliminatively, or perhaps even better than that. Take into account all cynical possibilities....

items.title: Waluigi World
items.content:
She was like the pause in the room but didn’t know it yet — pregnant.

Tatiana lit a cigarette. She had volunteered to speak first.

“Spring was late, and so was my period. Something has been going on recently. I invited over these two I met at a bookstore, a guy and a girl. The guy – as soon as he looked at me, I froze. My vulva was as cold as his heart. I was sitting down. She walked over to me. She came right up to me and pushed my head into her thighs. Her vagina was like a womb.”

Waluigi nodded wisely. Though it was his first time running a support group, Waluigi was a natural. Women, he felt, had always seemed comfortable in his presence. Perhaps he would consider a career as an OBGYN. Or maybe…

“We exchanged body fluids and ideas. She said she filled her god-shaped hole with Russian literature and American semen. That’s why she picked me – I’m writing my dissertation on Dostoevsky. She left me Dostoevsky’s Demons and for two and a half weeks. Eros kept me warm that night. Eros is that homeless guy that lives on twelfth street.

“The next night, the guy came back. ‘So you study the big D, eh?’ His joke was lame, like a person with a limp. I asked him about himself. His three favorite things in life were making money, love, and off with another man’s money. I told him about Eros. He passed judgement and then out. I guess his heart was as hard as his cock.”

Something stirred within Waluigi. “When were you expecting your period?”

“Let me think… Oh. Oh, I guess it should have come four weeks ago.”

Tatiana stared into space for a few seconds. “Hm.” She touched her headscarf, which was as red as the period that she didn’t have should have been. “I guess I’ve been so busy preparing for my master’s exam that I didn’t even think about that.” She smiled. “Well, it looks like I’m going to be a professor and a—”...

items.title: Not just a bystander, not anymore…
items.content:
One Saturday night this summer, I was leisurely walking down main street hand-in-hand on a date, when suddenly, I heard a commotion about 50 yards down a busy side street. It was too far away to make out what was happening or what was being said. But I figured it was fine since the side street had plenty of people walking up and down it.

Still, I couldn’t help but peer into the distance, transfixed, like a deer in the headlights.

There was an anime convention going on that weekend. Initially, my brain reasoned that a couple of cosplayers were recording a TikTok video or doing a K-pop dance. Then my brain reasoned that surely, on a crowded street, nothing serious could be going down. Right?

Yet I waited there, unmoving, alert.

My date was casually standing there eating a cookie. She innocently asked, “What do you think’s going on over there?”

I faintly heard a woman yelling. While squinting, I saw sudden, physical contact between her and a man. I dropped my date’s hand and began aggressively stomping towards them. 

All I could see was red.

I used to have anger problems during my adolescence. I didn't realize that maybe I was different from other people, until one day during my freshman year of college…

 

…I opened the door to my apartment to find a roomful of friends. One of them stood up from the couch to give me a hug with her arms outstretched, one hand high and the other hand low. I instinctually flinched, and then leaned in to give her a hug, but she pulled back and stopped. 

“I noticed that you always flinch before I give you a hug,” she said. “How come?”

I thought about it for a second, then copied her—one hand high and the other low—then nonchalantly said, “Your high hand? That’s probably the angle from which my dad hits me.”...
